<div class="markdown"><p>Chapters 1–5 learned from observations the learner did not choose. This chapter shows a case where no quantity of such observations is enough, but a single kind of action is.</p><p>We compare two mechanisms that generate a pair of coin flips. Watching many pairs cannot tell them apart, because they produce exactly the same distribution of pairs. Setting the first flip by hand and watching the second can. The paper makes the general point: when passive observation merges states that differ in the structure a task depends on, finding a representation that supports control may require acting on the world.</p></div>

<div class="markdown"><h2 id="Two-mechanisms">Two mechanisms</h2><p>In each episode, you receive a coin and see two flips. The coin model's parameters are the ones from Chapter 1.</p></div>

<div class="markdown"><p><strong>The hidden coin.</strong> This mechanism is Chapter 1's model: a friend picks a fair or trick coin, and both flips come from it independently. The two flips are correlated only because they share the coin.</p></div>


<div class="markdown"><p><strong>The sticky coin.</strong> A single coin lands heads with probability <code>marginal_heads</code>. After the first flip, with probability <code>stickiness</code>, the second flip copies the first; otherwise it is a fresh flip. Here the first flip causes the second.</p><p>We choose both numbers so that the sticky coin matches the hidden coin: the same probability of heads on the first flip, and the same probability of two heads.</p></div>

```julia
marginal_heads = is_fair_prior * fair_weight + (1 - is_fair_prior) * trick_weight
```

```text
0.675
```
{: .notebook-output}

```julia
both_heads = is_fair_prior * fair_weight^2 + (1 - is_fair_prior) * trick_weight^2
```

```text
0.48624999999999996
```
{: .notebook-output}

```julia
stickiness = both_heads / marginal_heads -
    (marginal_heads - both_heads) / (1 - marginal_heads)
```

```text
0.13960113960113907
```
{: .notebook-output}

<div class="markdown"><p><code>stickiness</code> is the difference between the probability of heads on the second flip after a head and after a tail, both under the hidden coin. At the starting settings it is about 0.14.</p></div>


<div class="markdown"><p>The two plots should look alike up to sampling noise. The next cell computes the exact probability of each pair under both mechanisms.</p></div>

```julia
function hidden_pair_probability(first, second)
    p(weight) = (first ? weight : 1 - weight) * (second ? weight : 1 - weight)
    is_fair_prior * p(fair_weight) + (1 - is_fair_prior) * p(trick_weight)
end
```

```julia
function sticky_pair_probability(first, second)
    p_first = first ? marginal_heads : 1 - marginal_heads
    p_fresh = second ? marginal_heads : 1 - marginal_heads
    p_first * (stickiness * (first == second) + (1 - stickiness) * p_fresh)
end
```

```julia
[(pair = show_pair(a, b),
  hidden_coin = hidden_pair_probability(a, b),
  sticky_coin = sticky_pair_probability(a, b))
 for a in (true, false) for b in (true, false)]
```

```text
4-element Vector{@NamedTuple{pair::String, hidden_coin::Float64, sticky_coin::Float64}}:
 (pair = "HH", hidden_coin = 0.48624999999999996, sticky_coin = 0.4862499999999999)
 (pair = "HT", hidden_coin = 0.18875, sticky_coin = 0.1887500000000001)
 (pair = "TH", hidden_coin = 0.18875, sticky_coin = 0.18875000000000008)
 (pair = "TT", hidden_coin = 0.13625, sticky_coin = 0.13624999999999987)
```
{: .notebook-output}

<div class="markdown"><p>The columns agree exactly, so any statistic of observed pairs has the same distribution under both mechanisms and watching pairs can never favour one of them. Conditioning does not help either: seeing a head first raises the probability of a second head to the same value in both models.</p></div>

```julia
(hidden_coin = mean(randsample(hidden_second |ᶜ hidden_first, 2000; alg = RejectionSample)),
 sticky_coin = mean(randsample(sticky_second |ᶜ sticky_first, 2000; alg = RejectionSample)),
 exact = both_heads / marginal_heads)
```

<div class="markdown"><h2 id="Setting-the-first-flip">Setting the first flip</h2><p>Now suppose you can place the first coin on the table heads up yourself, instead of flipping it. In Omega, <code>|ᵈ</code> acts as the <code>do</code>-operator. <code>sticky_second |ᵈ (sticky_first =&gt; true)</code> asks what the second flip would be if we set the first flip to heads.</p></div>

```julia
intervention_samples = 4000
```

```text
4000
```
{: .notebook-output}

```julia
intervention_table = [
    (mechanism = name,
     set_heads = mean(randsample(second |ᵈ (first => true), intervention_samples)),
     set_tails = mean(randsample(second |ᵈ (first => false), intervention_samples)))
    for (name, first, second) in [
        (:hidden_coin, hidden_first, hidden_second),
        (:sticky_coin, sticky_first, sticky_second),
    ]
]
```

```text
2-element Vector{@NamedTuple{mechanism::Symbol, set_heads::Float64, set_tails::Float64}}:
 (mechanism = :hidden_coin, set_heads = 0.68425, set_tails = 0.679)
 (mechanism = :sticky_coin, set_heads = 0.711, set_tails = 0.57)
```
{: .notebook-output}

<div class="markdown"><p>Under the hidden coin, setting the first flip changes nothing. The second flip does not depend on the first, so its probability of heads stays at <code>marginal_heads</code>, about 0.675, whichever value we set. Setting the first flip also cuts its link to the coin: an assigned head, unlike an observed one, says nothing about which coin we hold.</p><p>Under the sticky coin, the second flip follows the first. Setting heads gives about 0.72 and setting tails about 0.58, a difference equal to <code>stickiness</code>.</p><p>Try <code>trick_weight = 0.99</code>. Both mechanisms still match on pairs, but the gap under intervention grows.</p></div>

<div class="markdown"><h2 id="Learning-the-mechanism">Learning the mechanism</h2><p>A learner does not know which mechanism it faces and gives each probability one half. We generate episodes from the sticky coin and compare two learners. The passive learner watches pairs. The active learner sets the first flip at random in each episode and records the second.</p><p>Each episode uses a new coin, so episodes are independent.</p></div>

<div class="markdown"><p><code>controlled_probability</code> gives the probability of the second flip after we set the first, under each mechanism. The hidden coin ignores the setting; the sticky coin copies it with probability <code>stickiness</code>.</p></div>

```julia
function controlled_probability(mechanism, chosen, second)
    p_fresh = second ? marginal_heads : 1 - marginal_heads
    mechanism == :hidden_coin ? p_fresh :
        stickiness * (chosen == second) + (1 - stickiness) * p_fresh
end
```

```julia
function sticky_posterior(log_ratios)
    log_odds = sum(log_ratios; init = 0.0)
    1 / (1 + exp(-log_odds))
end
```

```julia
passive_log_ratios = [
    log(sticky_pair_probability(a, b)) - log(hidden_pair_probability(a, b))
    for (a, b) in passive_episodes
]
```

<div class="markdown"><p>The passive posterior stays at 0.5 however many episodes it sees. Every pair has the same probability under both mechanisms, so each log ratio is zero. The active posterior moves towards the sticky coin, usually past 0.9 by the last budget. Each intervention carries only a little evidence because <code>stickiness</code> is small; raise <code>trick_weight</code> to see it converge faster.</p><p>Set <code>true_mechanism = :hidden_coin</code>. The active posterior now moves towards the hidden coin, and the passive one still does not move.</p></div>

<div class="markdown"><h2 id="Prediction-and-control">Prediction and control</h2><p>The two mechanisms are equivalent for one task and different for another. To <em>predict</em> the second flip after seeing the first, the joint table of pairs is enough, and passive data estimate it well. To <em>control</em> the second flip, for example to make it land heads, you need to know whether setting the first flip has any effect. Only the mechanism answers that question.</p><p>Chapter 1 described a representation by the distinctions it keeps. Passive observation acts like a representation the learner cannot change: it keeps the pair of flips and nothing else. The distinction between the two mechanisms is not among the ones it keeps, because two different mechanisms produce the same observations. No amount of passive data can add that distinction. The action here is a transformation the learner applies to the world: setting the first flip. This helps distinguish between the mechanisms. </p><h2 id="Discussion">Discussion</h2><p>Watch three flips per episode instead of two. Under the hidden coin, <code>HTH</code> and <code>HHT</code> are equally likely. Are they under the sticky coin? What does your answer say about when passive data are enough?</p><p>Set <code>trick_weight = fair_weight</code>. What happens to <code>stickiness</code>, and why do the two mechanisms now agree under intervention as well?</p></div>
